To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
There is low quality evidence for the use of botulinum toxin A in chronic neck pain.

for chronic neck pain there is evidence of: a benefit from eperison hydrocholoride (moderate quality evidence, 1 trial); no benefit of botulinum toxin A compared to saline (high quality evidence, 5 trials); and no long-term effect of medial branch blocks of facet joints with corticosteroid compared to placebo (moderate quality of evidence, 1 study).

for chronic neck pain there was evidence of a small immediate benefit from eperison hydrochoride; no short-term pain relief from botulinum toxin A compared to saline nor from botulinum for subacute/ chronic whiplash; and no long term benefit from medial branch block of the facet joints with steroids over placebo to reduce neck pain or disability; and that there is no evidence for any other pharmacological interventions for chronic neck pain

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is no strong evidence for the use of pharmacological interventions for the treatment of neck pain.
there is a paucity of evidence to support or reject most pharmacological interventions.

there is a lack or insufficient evidence for most pharmacologic interventions for neck pain, with the exception of botulinum toxin for chronic neck pain and subacute/chronical whiplash, medial branch blocks for chronic facet joint neck pain and eperison hydrocholoride for chronic neck.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there is no evidence for most pharmacotherapies for neck pain and that there is no strong evidence to support the use of botulinum toxin A for chronic neck pain and subacute/chronical whiplash.
the current body of evidence is not sufficient to recommend any pharmacological intervention for acute or sub-acute neck pain, nor any for chronic neck pain with exception of eperison hydrocholoride.
there is a lack for high-quality evidence on the effects of pharmacological agents for neck pain, with the exception of eperison hydrocholoride.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is no evidence for many pharmacological interventions, and the evidence that does exist is not strong.
there are very limited data to support or refute the effectiveness of pharmacological interventions for acute and chronic neck pain.
